description: Hi!! We are the Buttered Croissants (by Lance, take up team name issues with him). We are UCL students. Please do not join our team - we are full. :c
summary:
The website we developed, Lance's Lookout, shows how any patch of the sky changes across SPHEREx's observations. The user enters a star name or sky coordinates, chooses a field of view, and the site finds every SPHEREx image of that position in the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). It cleans, aligns, and stacks the images by observing epoch, then plays the epochs as a blink. The three viewing modes (Frames, Difference, and Pair) make moving and variable objects stand out, and a spectrum panel compares brightness between epochs at matched wavelengths.

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, producing more data than any one person can examine. Moving objects, from asteroids and comets to brown dwarfs and possible undiscovered planets, are found by comparing images taken at different times, and volunteers have already discovered many comets and brown dwarfs this way. Lance's Lookout puts that comparison in a browser, with no need for any software installation. Every additional person looking raises the chance that something new is noticed, and a tool this easy to use lets a student in a classroom or a volunteer at home do the same kind of comparison that led to Pluto's discovery.
details:
Lance's Lookout lets anyone search across NASA's SPHEREx data to find objects that are moving or changing brightness. You type a star name (with suggestions and typo correction) or sky coordinates and the site plays a loop of every SPHEREx visit to that patch of sky. Blinking, the same method used to find pluto is applied to NASA's new infrared survey.

For any position, the server:
- Looks the name up in SIMBAD (via CDS Sesame), including the star’s proper motion, so fast-moving stars are centred where they actually were during SPHEREx’s observations.
- Queries NASA/IPAC’s IRSA archive for every SPHEREx image covering that spot and downloads small cutouts.
- Groups the images into epochs (separate visits). Each image is cleaned (zodiacal light subtracted, bad pixels removed) and re-projected onto one north-up grid.
Median-stacks each epoch and renders the frames on one shared brightness scale.

Lance’s Lookout removes the barriers to entry: students, amateur astronomers and citizen scientists can explore any part of the sky in a browser and see motion and variability for themselves. It lets researchers quickly check a candidate: a nearby brown dwarf, a variable star, or a distant object such as a hypothetical Planet X.

Tools used:
- Python: FastAPI, astropy, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, pyvo, Pillow.
- A single HTML/JavaScript web page.
- Docker, hosted on Render, with code on GitHub.
- The code was written with an AI coding assistant (Claude) under our team’s direction.

Creative aspects, features and other considerations:
Automatic detector choice - the site picks the best infrared band for each target.
Fair band combining: detectors are combined so every frame holds the same mix of wavelengths.
A spectrum that follows the blink - the live spectrum is synchronised with the animation and compares epochs at matched wavelengths.
Usability - name suggestions, clear errors, keyboard controls and shareable links.
Reliability - NASA’s archive was intermittently down during the hackathon, so the site falls back to cached data and pre-built targets.
Cost and access - free hosting and open-source tools, so anyone can run or extend it.
